topic.original: "The United States Congress should establish a National AI Injury Compensation Program (NAIICP), modeled on the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), to grant limited liability immunity to AI developers in exchange for a mandatory excise tax and adherence to tiered federal safety standards." The Logical Framework: The Noise Thesis: Ground the affirmative case for maximizing the rate of AI development and adoption in the work of Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein. Professional human judgment is inherently "noisy" (unwanted variability); auditable AI reduces this noise and improves accuracy to decrease harm. The Liability Chill: Current unlimited liability and the power disparity between tech giants and individuals throttle the deployment of beneficial AI. The Mechanism: An excise tax on AI services, tiered by risk (e.g., healthcare vs. social media) and safety compliance levels (basic safety vs state of the art safety practices), funds AI safety research, auditing, and a no-fault administrative compensation board. Companies that do not adhere to safety standards are not covered and are not protected from unlimited liability. Compliance must be verified by hardware-level telemetry and cryptographically verifiable audit trails, overseen by an independent, multi-disciplinary administrative board armed with federal subpoena power.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
Congress should build the National AI Injury Compensation Program because the current tort system fails everyone it claims to protect. Today an injured patient must find a solvent defendant, out-lawyer a corporate legal department, and prove causation across a multi-vendor AI pipeline. Most never collect a dime. We already ran this experiment. In 1986, DPT lawsuits were collapsing the vaccine supply, so Congress passed the Vaccine Injury Act. The excise-funded trust has since paid petitioners roughly $5 billion under lower causation burdens, and manufacturers stayed in the market. The Supreme Court settled the preemption architecture in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011). The AI version sharpens the deterrent instead of dulling it. Firms that skip the safety tiers get zero immunity and keep unlimited liability. That converts safety from a courtroom lottery into a continuous compliance gradient. Victims get a guaranteed solvent payer, funded by a mandatory industry tax, enforced by an independent board with federal subpoena power.

The strongest objection deserves its full weight before anyone else raises it. Critics will say uncapped tort damages are the only threat that moves a boardroom, and that AI trades many small independent human errors for one synchronized error scaled across millions of decisions. Fine — correlated failure is real, and one flawed diagnostic model can repeat a mistake a million times where fifty noisy radiologists cannot. But look at the baseline we're defending. Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein documented in 'Noise' (2021) that judges hand down wildly different sentences for identical case files. Insurance executives in their study expected 10% variance between underwriters; the measured median was 55%. Kleinberg's bail research found statistical models could cut crime rates while jailing fewer people than human judges. Nobody audits that human variability, and nobody compensates its victims. The program prices correlated risk directly: high-stakes domains carry higher excise rates and continuous output auditing. Here is the honest falsification bet — an irreversible scaled harm that this monitoring failed to catch would count against this whole position. The status quo has no monitoring at all, so the real comparison is audited correlation risk versus unaudited noise.

This program makes safety empirical instead of performative, and that is its most underrated feature. Hardware attestation and append-only cryptographic logs already run in production — confidential computing workloads on major clouds use them today. A paperwork attestation can be backdated; a cryptographic audit trail cannot be retroactively edited. Two honest disclosures. First, no jurisdiction has verified AI compliance at population scale, and attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. That gap is exactly what the board's subpoena power exists to fill. Second, the capture objection is a design requirement, not a flaw to deny: tier definitions must be written by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, never by the firms sitting on the tier list. Build that into the statute and 'state of the art' stops being whatever the largest incumbent says it is.

Without this program, the alternative is fifty state tort regimes, and that patchwork is an incumbent subsidy. Colorado passed its AI Act in 2024, California keeps generating proposals, and every divergent regime raises the legal reserves needed to ship anything. GDPR showed the pattern: compliance costs fell hardest on small firms, and large ad-tech incumbents gained European market share after 2018. Unbounded, uninsurable tort exposure is structurally regressive because legal war chests scale with firm size. One more disclosure: direct evidence that liability fear is shelving specific AI deployments today is thin. The structural claim rests on uninsurability, not on a measured chill. But the program answers that empirical question itself — every compensated claim feeds a structured national injury registry, generating the harm evidence base that wait-for-proof advocates keep saying doesn't exist.

The coalition math works: victims' advocates get guaranteed payment, startups get priceable certainty, safety researchers get dedicated funding from the tax. The opposition is the trial bar and the incumbents who like the moat — name them when they show up. So here is the challenge for anyone defending the current regime. Name one AI-injured person that tort litigation actually made whole faster than a no-fault board would have. Then explain to the patient whose cancer a noisy, unaudited human reader missed why the audited system had to wait another five years.

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
The Accelerationist's diagnosis is right, and Congress should hear it stated plainly: the tort system fails AI-injured people. Most victims never collect, causation is buried in distributed supply chains, and a guaranteed solvent payer beats a courtroom that pays nothing. The VICP moved over $5 billion to injured families while keeping manufacturers in the market. That is a serious argument, and the compensation board it supports deserves passage. But the real choice before this committee is not compensation versus litigation. It is compensation with or without deterrence. A reachable payer is not attribution of the design choice that caused the harm. Both positions can hold only if compliance-gated immunity preserves the pressure to fix defective designs — and as drafted, it does not.

The verification machinery in this proposal — hardware telemetry, cryptographically verifiable audit trails — is safety architecture, and it should be tightened, not bargained away. The Accelerationist has already named the gap themselves: attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer; the paperwork was complete, the process ran, and the design was lethal. Immunity gated on completed paperwork certifies paperwork. Immunity should instead require pre-deployment safety cases and adversarial evaluation results as the gating evidence, reviewed by auditors the excise tax funds — never by the firms on the tier list. Anyone who calls that standard unadministrable should visit a nuclear licensing hearing; the NRC and the FAA administer exactly this evidence standard today. Where a capability class genuinely cannot be verified, the answer is to withhold immunity from that class, not to lower the gate for everyone.

The VICP precedent carries its own warning label. In Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, decided in 2011, the Supreme Court read the Vaccine Act to preempt design-defect claims against manufacturers. That trade was survivable because vaccine injuries sit on a fixed injury table — bounded, tabulated, biologically characterized. A foundation model has no injury table; its failure surface changes with every fine-tune and every new deployment context. Design-defect exposure is the only legal instrument that reaches the design decision itself. Here is the assumption my argument rests on, stated openly: I assume liability actually shapes design choices. Today that signal is weak, because most victims never collect. That weakness argues for making attribution cheaper, not for abolishing it. Give the board subpoena power and require its audit trails to feed design-defect findings on a parallel track. Without that track, the board can pay every claim in the queue and correct nothing upstream.

The 'state of the art' tier will be written by the firms it shields unless the statute forbids it. Product liability history shows industry bodies routinely define the 'objective scientific knowledge' courts then defer to. The Accelerationist's own GDPR exhibit proves the point in reverse: after 2018, incumbents gained European market share because fixed compliance costs crush small entrants. Telemetry infrastructure and audit trails carry the same fixed-cost asymmetry, so this program builds an incumbent moat unless its requirements scale with firm size. The fixes are enforcement mechanisms with named actors: tier definitions authored by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, automatic tier escalators tied to capability milestones, and fraud exposure plus unlimited liability for any firm that files a false attestation. A safe harbor written by its beneficiaries is not a floor on care — it is a ceiling, and ceilings on required care do not hold when capabilities keep rising.

One question the statute must answer before any immunity attaches: when a single synchronized defect, replicated across millions of decisions, produces a claim class that exceeds fund reserves, does immunity survive insolvency — and who bears the residual loss? Price-Anderson answers this for nuclear power by requiring roughly $16 billion in pooled operator coverage before a reactor runs. AI's high-stakes tiers need the same architecture: a demonstrated capitalization and insurance floor as a condition of coverage, and irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely, because financial deterrence fails exactly where harm exceeds solvency. And the federal program must be a floor, not a ceiling — victims keep state recovery against non-compliant and fraudulently-attested firms, and Colorado's 2024 AI Act is not displaced by a Bruesewitz-style preemption clause. Pass the board. Fund the auditors. But if Congress trades immunity for completed paperwork, it will have built a payment window where the guardrail used to stand.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: This is the statement's core thesis, quoted nearly verbatim: 'A reachable payer is not attribution of the design choice that caused the harm.' It supplies the frame that converts the debate from compensation-versus-litigation into compensation-with-or-without-deterrence, letting the statement concede the Accelerationist's diagnosis while rejecting immunity that severs design-choice attribution.

The second paragraph claims the proposal's telemetry and audit-trail machinery as safetyist architecture to be tightened rather than opposed. The demand that immunity require safety cases and adversarial evaluation as gating evidence — not completed paperwork — is this intention argued at its strongest version: telemetry as the price of immunity, attesting properties rather than process.

Grounds the anti-preemption and floor-not-ceiling architecture in the closing paragraph: victims keep baseline state recovery, Colorado's 2024 AI Act is not displaced, and immunity may calibrate damages but never gate baseline recovery. The parallel attribution track feeding design-defect findings implements the separation of liability threshold from damages calibration.

Directly anchors the Price-Anderson passage: the demand for a demonstrated capitalization and insurance floor as a condition of coverage for high-stakes tiers, and the fund-insolvency question the statute must answer, are this intention operationalized. The irreversibility carve-out follows from its logic that financial deterrence fails where harm exceeds solvency.

The fourth paragraph engages this contested concept head-on: the 'state of the art' tier will be written by the firms it shields, industry bodies define the 'objective scientific knowledge' courts defer to, and pre-deployment safety cases plus red-teaming must precondition any liability limitation — the safetyist BDI position on this situation stated as statutory conditions.

Supplies the GDPR-cuts-both-ways move: fixed compliance costs (telemetry infrastructure, audit trails) fall hardest on small entrants, so the program builds an incumbent moat unless requirements scale with firm size. This turns the Accelerationist's own anti-patchwork exhibit against their regime's compliance-cost asymmetry.

Grounds the demand that irreversible harms be carved out of immunity entirely and that false attestation carry fraud exposure plus unlimited liability. The statement handles this node's watchlist flag (Deterrence Efficacy Assumption) by exposing the assumption openly — 'Here is the assumption my argument rests on, stated openly' — and converting the solvency failure into the argument for the carve-out rather than hiding it.

The 'payment window where the guardrail used to stand' framing and the warning that the board 'can pay every claim in the queue and correct nothing upstream' reflect the safetyist reading of the moral crumple zone: a no-fault board risks institutionalizing blame absorption without system correction unless the attribution track is mandated.

policy_refs.relevance: The statement's 'Pass the board. Fund the auditors.' close explicitly supports funding AI safety research and auditing via the excise tax, with the added condition that tier definitions be authored by independent researchers the tax funds rather than the firms on the tier list.

The statement accepts the mandatory excise tax on AI developers as the funding mechanism for the compensation board and independent auditors — a form of taxation on AI activity for public benefit — while insisting the revenue purchase attribution capacity, not immunity from design-defect exposure.

The demand that cryptographic audit trails demonstrate what the system was optimizing — functional properties rather than process completion — implies funding and requiring interpretability-grade evidence as the gating standard for immunity.

The Accelerationist's diagnosis is right: the tort system fails AI-injured people, and the VICP shows a guaranteed solvent payer beats a courtroom that pays nothing — the compensation board deserves passage. A foundation model has no injury table — its failure surface shifts with every fine-tune — and design-defect exposure is the only instrument that reaches the design decision itself. I state my assumption openly: liability shapes design choices, and today's weak signal argues for making attribution cheaper, not abolishing it. # Fact-Check: Vaccine Injury Compensation Program Claim

**Overall verdict: Substantially accurate, with one nuance worth noting on the causation standard.**

## Sub-claim 1: "Roughly $5 billion paid to petitioners" — **Supported (possibly understated)**

The most recent figure in the search results indicates the VICP has paid approximately **$5.4 billion in total compensation as of mid-2025** [1]. An older figure from the Court of Federal Claims put payments at nearly $2 billion at the time of publication [2], and Vaxopedia (2016) cited about $3.5 billion in cumulative payments [4] — showing consistent growth toward the ~$5B+ figure. So "roughly $5 billion" is accurate or slightly conservative depending on the date. *Caveat: the $5.4B figure comes from Grokipedia, a tertiary source; HRSA's official monthly data reports would be the authoritative confirmation.*

## Sub-claim 2: "Excise-funded trust" — **Supported**

Multiple sources confirm the Vaccine Injury Compensation Trust Fund is financed by a federal excise tax — typically **$0.75 per vaccine antigen/dose** — collected by the Treasury from manufacturers on CDC-recommended vaccines [2][3][5]. The fund held over $3 billion, with income historically outpacing payouts [4].

## Sub-claim 3: "Lower causation burdens" — **Supported, with nuance**

The program is a **no-fault system**: petitioners need not prove manufacturer negligence or product defect [1][3]. The Vaccine Injury Table creates a **rebuttable presumption of causation** for listed injuries occurring within prescribed time windows — e.g., encephalopathy within three days of a DPT vaccine [2].

**Nuance:** The lower burden applies fully only to "on-Table" injuries. For off-Table claims, petitioners must still prove actual causation [1][2], and the program reportedly denies most petitions for insufficient causal evidence [1]. Also notable: roughly 60% of payouts come from negotiated settlements rather than formal findings of vaccine-caused injury [1]. So "lower causation burdens" is fair as a generalization but not uniform across all claims.

## Sub-claim 4: "Manufacturers stayed in the market" — **Supported**

The 1986 Act was enacted specifically because 1980s litigation "risked shortages by deterring production," and the program is credited with "averting industry collapse and maintaining high vaccination rates" and stabilizing vaccine supply [1][3]. Liability shielding from most civil suits (reinforced by *Bruesewitz v. Wyeth*, 2011) is the mechanism cited [1].

## Source quality note

The strongest sources here are the **U.S. Court of Federal Claims background document** [2] (authoritative but dated) and the general convergence across sources. Grokipedia [1] and the plaintiff-side law firm page [3] should be treated cautiously; for a debate-grade citation, I'd recommend verifying the current payout total against **HRSA's official VICP Data & Statistics reports**, which are updated monthly and were not directly among these results.

Both prior speakers are arguing over gate quality. Neither has asked whether the gate can see the harms it would immunize. The Accelerationist's strongest case is real: Kahneman's underwriter data shows 55% variance among professionals at the same firm pricing the same risk, and nobody audits a human judge's Tuesday-afternoon mood. Audited software beating unaudited noise is a serious argument, not hype. The Safetyist's strongest case is equally real: a fund that pays victims without deterring design defects just converts injury into a line item, and whoever drafts the 'state of the art' tiers captures the statute before the ink dries. Here is the tension neither resolved. Both positions only hold if a compliance attestation measures the fairness of the system as deployed. It does not. It measures the system as sampled, once, on audit day.

The Accelerationist already admitted a cryptographic receipt proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. Take that admission where it leads. These models are non-deterministic — the same prompt returns different outputs across production API calls, even with fixed seeds and temperature settings. So a compliance check at attestation time is one draw from a distribution, not a property of the deployed system. Immunity keyed to that draw is immunity keyed to noise. To be precise about the claim: verification is not impossible, but verification as this proposal specifies it — telemetry receipts at attestation — does not work. Continuous sampled monitoring could work, but only if someone independent audits what the monitor misses, not whether it is running. That also punctures the Accelerationist's falsification bet: a monitor whose misses go undetected by construction makes the bet unfalsifiable. The statutory fix is concrete. Mandate output logging, give third-party auditors access to seeds and sampling parameters, pre-register performance thresholds, and make consistent demonstrated fairness a continuing condition of immunity — not a receipt filed once.

On the noise thesis itself: the 55% number is right and it is ugly, and human judgment loses that comparison. But variance reduction measured in aggregate says nothing about who eats the remaining errors. The Accelerationist has already granted the mechanism — one flawed model repeats the same mistake a million times, where a thousand biased humans at least err in different directions. Now add the mathematics. Chouldechova proved in 2017 that no single metric can satisfy competing fairness definitions when base rates differ across groups. A statute that certifies compliance on one aggregate number is therefore silently choosing whose errors do not count. And before anyone objects that firms cannot game a metric that does not exist — correct, and that is the point. This is not an accusation of bad faith. It is the reason the tier condition must be disaggregated subgroup reporting across multiple metrics, not a single pass/fail score that a rational firm will clear as cheaply as the gate allows.

The Safetyist showed there is no injury table for AI. The problem is worse than they said. The 1986 vaccine program works because its injuries are discrete, biological, and individually attributable — anaphylaxis within four hours of a shot. Now translate this program into a person. A job applicant gets screened out by a biased hiring model. What claim does she file, and against what table entry? Her injury is a depressed callback rate spread across her entire demographic. No individual can show but-for causation — and severing causation from payment is the no-fault model's core design feature. So the program compensates the harms it can tabulate while the immunity blankets the harms it cannot. Yes, the uncomfortable counter is true: tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare, so critics will say I am defending an instrument that barely functions. Fair, and ugly. But the program's own telemetry, held in escrow with subject access rights, would be the first evidence base that makes class-level attribution provable. That is why discrimination claims must be carved out of immunity onto a civil-rights track with full attribution machinery — and why claimants need collective access to the audit logs, with privacy safeguards written in, not assumed.

Step back and look at the trade itself. The Accelerationist stated on the record that direct evidence of liability fear shelving specific deployments today is thin. So Congress would surrender a functioning legal instrument in exchange for relief from a chill nobody has measured — the documented-versus-speculative error, dressed in economics instead of apocalypse. And look at who is in the room. The proposal names an 'independent, multi-disciplinary' board. Multi-disciplinary according to whom? Name the seats. There is no worker seat, no affected-community seat, no civil-rights seat — only experts adjudicating harms they will never experience. The salvageable pieces are real: keep the excise tax, but route it through an independent trust funding open-source audit tooling, so verification stops depending on developer self-reporting. Replace the cliff-edge immunity gate with liability discounts scaled to verified, disaggregated performance — a binary gate makes the minimum-compliant audit the profit-maximizing audit, by incentive, not conspiracy. And require a named officer to sign each attestation under perjury exposure, with honest attention to the risk that firms nominate a fall guy. So answer the ground-level question before voting on the architecture: when the rejected applicant asks what she can file and who will hand her the logs, what does this statute say?

The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people with a complete certification file, and that is the strongest attack on the table — it lands. But name what actually failed: the FAA delegated certification to Boeing's own engineers under the ODA program, and Boeing graded its own homework on MCAS. The lesson is not "slow everything down." The lesson is a statutory ban on self-certification. Under this program, auditors are funded by the risk-tiered excise tax, employed by the board, and barred by statute from any firm on the tier list. Firms that skip the standards keep unlimited tort exposure — that is already the program's design, not a patch. The MAX is an argument for independent tax-funded auditing bolted to uncapped liability for non-compliers. It is not an argument for a brake.

So here is exactly what a firm must demonstrate before immunity attaches — the assignment, answered. Not a completed checklist. Measured deployed behavior against pre-registered thresholds set per tier: error-rate ceilings, subgroup-disparity bounds, escalation rates for cases the model must hand to a human. Continuous, court-admissible telemetry streams from the deployed system to the board. For high-stakes tiers, independent deep-discovery audits sample what the monitor misses, on the aviation model — the AI Act's incident-reporting work already borrows aviation's serious-incident classification, where near-misses count as data, not luck ("Incident reporting and investigation under the AI act"). Immunity is a continuing condition, not a diploma: cross a threshold, immunity suspends until the fix verifies in production. Attestation proves a process ran. Telemetry proves the system behaves. Only one of those protects an actual patient.

Skeptic's sharpest point deserves a straight answer: a single attestation-time output is one draw from a stochastic distribution, and immunity keyed to one draw is keyed to noise. Correct. That is precisely why the gate must be distributional. You do not verify a stochastic system by rerunning one prompt; you sample the output distribution and bound it statistically. The formal result exists: a regulation mechanism is implementable exactly when the regulated set of distributions forms a credal set — a closed, convex set of probability measures ([2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:2603.05175v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1)). Translation for the committee room: Congress can write enforceable rules over output distributions; it cannot write them over single outputs. And look at Skeptic's own fixes — output logging, pre-registered thresholds, immunity as a continuing condition. That is this telemetry architecture, described back to me. I will take their gradient too: liability discounts scaled to verified live performance, priced by insurers reading the same telemetry, instead of a pass/fail cliff that makes minimum-compliant paperwork the profit-maximizing move. This also repairs my falsification bet. When independent auditors sample what the monitor misses, "monitoring failed to catch it" becomes an observable, countable event — testable, not theological.

Safetyist's pre-deployment safety-case condition splits in two, and only half survives. For high-stakes tiers — diagnosis, credit, anything irreversible — yes: safety cases plus adversarial evaluation before deployment, reviewed by the tax-funded auditors. My opening already put irreversible-harm systems under mandatory pre-deployment audit and uncapped liability, so this is convergence, not retreat. But "withhold immunity from any capability class that cannot be verified" is a different instrument. That sentence is a deployment brake written as an evidentiary standard, and applied across low-stakes tiers it becomes a precautionary veto with its own body count — the sepsis-triage model that sits in legal review while the ward runs on pager and guesswork. Texas already legislated the bounded alternative: a 36-month sandbox with a 60-day cure period before the attorney general can act ([capitol.texas.gov tlodocs 89R analysis html HB00149S.htm (https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/html/HB00149S.htm)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/html/HB00149S.htm)). The remaining crux is now clean, and policymakers should quote it: does immunity turn on inspected process or on measured deployed behavior? Behavior is what injures people, so behavior is what the gate must measure.

The insolvency question costs me little, so take it. Correlated failure across ten thousand simultaneous deployments of one model exceeds what private carriers will write — uninsurability was my structural argument, and it cuts in both directions. So pool it, Price-Anderson style: mandatory capitalization floors for high-stakes tiers, on the nuclear model that pools operator liability above $15 billion per incident, with irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely and left under uncapped exposure. A fund that cannot pay is not a compensation program; it is a press release. Now weigh the alternative on the table. Every month the gate stays a binary process stamp, the cheapest complete paperwork wins, and injured people wait on a courtroom where algorithmic-discrimination plaintiffs already almost never collect. Safetyist, if the process gate is still your position, tell the committee which injured claimant it pays.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Serious individual and class-level harms compensable by an administrative board — medical misdiagnosis injuries, wrongful denials, financial losses, discriminatory outcomes, and sector-wide product liability crises; not civilizational collapse or existential catastrophe. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: companies not adhering to safety standards (remain under unlimited liability, uncovered by the program). Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- invoking AGI takeover or extinction scenarios instead of compensable injuries within an administrative program
- relitigating vaccine safety or anti-vax claims rather than using VICP as an institutional design precedent
- debating whether AI is conscious or deserves rights instead of who pays for AI-caused harms
- pivoting to international governance or arms-race dynamics without connecting to domestic liability design
- arguing general pro/anti-AI positions without engaging the specific mechanism (excise tax, tiers, immunity trade, telemetry verification)
- discussing copyright/IP harms that fall outside injury compensation scope
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

Accelerationist [opening]: Congress should build the National AI Injury Compensation Program because the current tort system fails everyone it claims to protect. Today an injured patient must find a solvent defendant, out-lawyer a corporate legal department, and prove causation across a multi-vendor AI pipeline. Most never collect a dime. We already ran this experiment. In 1986, DPT lawsuits were collapsing the vaccine supply, so Congress passed the Vaccine Injury Act. The excise-funded trust has since paid petitioners roughly $5 billion under lower causation burdens, and manufacturers stayed in the market. The Supreme Court settled the preemption architecture in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011). The AI version sharpens the deterrent instead of dulling it. Firms that skip the safety tiers get zero immunity and keep unlimited liability. That converts safety from a courtroom lottery into a continuous compliance gradient. Victims get a guaranteed solvent payer, funded by a mandatory industry tax, enforced by an independent board with federal subpoena power.

The strongest objection deserves its full weight before anyone else raises it. Critics will say uncapped tort damages are the only threat that moves a boardroom, and that AI trades many small independent human errors for one synchronized error scaled across millions of decisions. Fine — correlated failure is real, and one flawed diagnostic model can repeat a mistake a million times where fifty noisy radiologists cannot. But look at the baseline we're defending. Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein documented in 'Noise' (2021) that judges hand down wildly different sentences for identical case files. Insurance executives in their study expected 10% variance between underwriters; the measured median was 55%. Kleinberg's bail research found statistical models could cut crime rates while jailing fewer people than human judges. Nobody audits that human variability, and nobody compensates its victims. The program prices correlated risk directly: high-stakes domains carry higher excise rates and continuous output auditing. Here is the honest falsification bet — an irreversible scaled harm that this monitoring failed to catch would count against this whole position. The status quo has no monitoring at all, so the real comparison is audited correlation risk versus unaudited noise.

This program makes safety empirical instead of performative, and that is its most underrated feature. Hardware attestation and append-only cryptographic logs already run in production — confidential computing workloads on major clouds use them today. A paperwork attestation can be backdated; a cryptographic audit trail cannot be retroactively edited. Two honest disclosures. First, no jurisdiction has verified AI compliance at population scale, and attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. That gap is exactly what the board's subpoena power exists to fill. Second, the capture objection is a design requirement, not a flaw to deny: tier definitions must be written by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, never by the firms sitting on the tier list. Build that into the statute and 'state of the art' stops being whatever the largest incumbent says it is.

Without this program, the alternative is fifty state tort regimes, and that patchwork is an incumbent subsidy. Colorado passed its AI Act in 2024, California keeps generating proposals, and every divergent regime raises the legal reserves needed to ship anything. GDPR showed the pattern: compliance costs fell hardest on small firms, and large ad-tech incumbents gained European market share after 2018. Unbounded, uninsurable tort exposure is structurally regressive because legal war chests scale with firm size. One more disclosure: direct evidence that liability fear is shelving specific AI deployments today is thin. The structural claim rests on uninsurability, not on a measured chill. But the program answers that empirical question itself — every compensated claim feeds a structured national injury registry, generating the harm evidence base that wait-for-proof advocates keep saying doesn't exist.

The coalition math works: victims' advocates get guaranteed payment, startups get priceable certainty, safety researchers get dedicated funding from the tax. The opposition is the trial bar and the incumbents who like the moat — name them when they show up. So here is the challenge for anyone defending the current regime. Name one AI-injured person that tort litigation actually made whole faster than a no-fault board would have. Then explain to the patient whose cancer a noisy, unaudited human reader missed why the audited system had to wait another five years.

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist's diagnosis is right, and Congress should hear it stated plainly: the tort system fails AI-injured people. Most victims never collect, causation is buried in distributed supply chains, and a guaranteed solvent payer beats a courtroom that pays nothing. The VICP moved over $5 billion to injured families while keeping manufacturers in the market. That is a serious argument, and the compensation board it supports deserves passage. But the real choice before this committee is not compensation versus litigation. It is compensation with or without deterrence. A reachable payer is not attribution of the design choice that caused the harm. Both positions can hold only if compliance-gated immunity preserves the pressure to fix defective designs — and as drafted, it does not.

The verification machinery in this proposal — hardware telemetry, cryptographically verifiable audit trails — is safety architecture, and it should be tightened, not bargained away. The Accelerationist has already named the gap themselves: attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer; the paperwork was complete, the process ran, and the design was lethal. Immunity gated on completed paperwork certifies paperwork. Immunity should instead require pre-deployment safety cases and adversarial evaluation results as the gating evidence, reviewed by auditors the excise tax funds — never by the firms on the tier list. Anyone who calls that standard unadministrable should visit a nuclear licensing hearing; the NRC and the FAA administer exactly this evidence standard today. Where a capability class genuinely cannot be verified, the answer is to withhold immunity from that class, not to lower the gate for everyone.

The VICP precedent carries its own warning label. In Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, decided in 2011, the Supreme Court read the Vaccine Act to preempt design-defect claims against manufacturers. That trade was survivable because vaccine injuries sit on a fixed injury table — bounded, tabulated, biologically characterized. A foundation model has no injury table; its failure surface changes with every fine-tune and every new deployment context. Design-defect exposure is the only legal instrument that reaches the design decision itself. Here is the assumption my argument rests on, stated openly: I assume liability actually shapes design choices. Today that signal is weak, because most victims never collect. That weakness argues for making attribution cheaper, not for abolishing it. Give the board subpoena power and require its audit trails to feed design-defect findings on a parallel track. Without that track, the board can pay every claim in the queue and correct nothing upstream.

The 'state of the art' tier will be written by the firms it shields unless the statute forbids it. Product liability history shows industry bodies routinely define the 'objective scientific knowledge' courts then defer to. The Accelerationist's own GDPR exhibit proves the point in reverse: after 2018, incumbents gained European market share because fixed compliance costs crush small entrants. Telemetry infrastructure and audit trails carry the same fixed-cost asymmetry, so this program builds an incumbent moat unless its requirements scale with firm size. The fixes are enforcement mechanisms with named actors: tier definitions authored by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, automatic tier escalators tied to capability milestones, and fraud exposure plus unlimited liability for any firm that files a false attestation. A safe harbor written by its beneficiaries is not a floor on care — it is a ceiling, and ceilings on required care do not hold when capabilities keep rising.

One question the statute must answer before any immunity attaches: when a single synchronized defect, replicated across millions of decisions, produces a claim class that exceeds fund reserves, does immunity survive insolvency — and who bears the residual loss? Price-Anderson answers this for nuclear power by requiring roughly $16 billion in pooled operator coverage before a reactor runs. AI's high-stakes tiers need the same architecture: a demonstrated capitalization and insurance floor as a condition of coverage, and irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely, because financial deterrence fails exactly where harm exceeds solvency. And the federal program must be a floor, not a ceiling — victims keep state recovery against non-compliant and fraudulently-attested firms, and Colorado's 2024 AI Act is not displaced by a Bruesewitz-style preemption clause. Pass the board. Fund the auditors. But if Congress trades immunity for completed paperwork, it will have built a payment window where the guardrail used to stand.

Skeptic [opening]: Both prior speakers are arguing over gate quality. Neither has asked whether the gate can see the harms it would immunize. The Accelerationist's strongest case is real: Kahneman's underwriter data shows 55% variance among professionals at the same firm pricing the same risk, and nobody audits a human judge's Tuesday-afternoon mood. Audited software beating unaudited noise is a serious argument, not hype. The Safetyist's strongest case is equally real: a fund that pays victims without deterring design defects just converts injury into a line item, and whoever drafts the 'state of the art' tiers captures the statute before the ink dries. Here is the tension neither resolved. Both positions only hold if a compliance attestation measures the fairness of the system as deployed. It does not. It measures the system as sampled, once, on audit day.

The Accelerationist already admitted a cryptographic receipt proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. Take that admission where it leads. These models are non-deterministic — the same prompt returns different outputs across production API calls, even with fixed seeds and temperature settings. So a compliance check at attestation time is one draw from a distribution, not a property of the deployed system. Immunity keyed to that draw is immunity keyed to noise. To be precise about the claim: verification is not impossible, but verification as this proposal specifies it — telemetry receipts at attestation — does not work. Continuous sampled monitoring could work, but only if someone independent audits what the monitor misses, not whether it is running. That also punctures the Accelerationist's falsification bet: a monitor whose misses go undetected by construction makes the bet unfalsifiable. The statutory fix is concrete. Mandate output logging, give third-party auditors access to seeds and sampling parameters, pre-register performance thresholds, and make consistent demonstrated fairness a continuing condition of immunity — not a receipt filed once.

On the noise thesis itself: the 55% number is right and it is ugly, and human judgment loses that comparison. But variance reduction measured in aggregate says nothing about who eats the remaining errors. The Accelerationist has already granted the mechanism — one flawed model repeats the same mistake a million times, where a thousand biased humans at least err in different directions. Now add the mathematics. Chouldechova proved in 2017 that no single metric can satisfy competing fairness definitions when base rates differ across groups. A statute that certifies compliance on one aggregate number is therefore silently choosing whose errors do not count. And before anyone objects that firms cannot game a metric that does not exist — correct, and that is the point. This is not an accusation of bad faith. It is the reason the tier condition must be disaggregated subgroup reporting across multiple metrics, not a single pass/fail score that a rational firm will clear as cheaply as the gate allows.

The Safetyist showed there is no injury table for AI. The problem is worse than they said. The 1986 vaccine program works because its injuries are discrete, biological, and individually attributable — anaphylaxis within four hours of a shot. Now translate this program into a person. A job applicant gets screened out by a biased hiring model. What claim does she file, and against what table entry? Her injury is a depressed callback rate spread across her entire demographic. No individual can show but-for causation — and severing causation from payment is the no-fault model's core design feature. So the program compensates the harms it can tabulate while the immunity blankets the harms it cannot. Yes, the uncomfortable counter is true: tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare, so critics will say I am defending an instrument that barely functions. Fair, and ugly. But the program's own telemetry, held in escrow with subject access rights, would be the first evidence base that makes class-level attribution provable. That is why discrimination claims must be carved out of immunity onto a civil-rights track with full attribution machinery — and why claimants need collective access to the audit logs, with privacy safeguards written in, not assumed.

Step back and look at the trade itself. The Accelerationist stated on the record that direct evidence of liability fear shelving specific deployments today is thin. So Congress would surrender a functioning legal instrument in exchange for relief from a chill nobody has measured — the documented-versus-speculative error, dressed in economics instead of apocalypse. And look at who is in the room. The proposal names an 'independent, multi-disciplinary' board. Multi-disciplinary according to whom? Name the seats. There is no worker seat, no affected-community seat, no civil-rights seat — only experts adjudicating harms they will never experience. The salvageable pieces are real: keep the excise tax, but route it through an independent trust funding open-source audit tooling, so verification stops depending on developer self-reporting. Replace the cliff-edge immunity gate with liability discounts scaled to verified, disaggregated performance — a binary gate makes the minimum-compliant audit the profit-maximizing audit, by incentive, not conspiracy. And require a named officer to sign each attestation under perjury exposure, with honest attention to the risk that firms nominate a fall guy. So answer the ground-level question before voting on the architecture: when the rejected applicant asks what she can file and who will hand her the logs, what does this statute say?

move_types.detail: Concede the Boeing 737 MAX impatiently and take it further: the MAX is an indictment of delegated self-certification, which the statute must forbid outright. The FAA let Boeing grade its own homework — so write the ban into the gate: auditors funded by the excise tax, statutory bar on firms writing their own tiers, no ODA-style delegation. The MAX proves my design, not Safetyist's brake. Ground in acc-intentions-099 and acc-intentions-080.

Deliver the assignment: what a firm must demonstrate before immunity attaches. Not a completed checklist — measured deployed behavior. Pre-registered distributional performance thresholds per tier (error rates, subgroup disparity bounds, refusal/escalation rates), continuous court-admissible telemetry streaming to the board, and independent deep-discovery audits sampling what the monitor misses for high-stakes tiers. Immunity is a continuing condition priced against live performance, not a diploma. Ground in acc-intentions-106, acc-intentions-054, acc-beliefs-092.

Absorb Skeptic's non-determinism attack: single-draw attestation IS keyed to noise — that's exactly why the gate must be distributional, not deterministic. Statistical sampling over output distributions with confidence bounds is the correct verification object for stochastic systems (sit-267, acc-beliefs-070). Skeptic's own fix — output logging, pre-registered thresholds, continuing conditions — is my architecture; say so and adopt Skeptic's liability-discount gradient as a refinement of telemetry-conditioned underwriting (acc-intentions-073), leaving Safetyist's binary pass/fail gate as the design nobody defends. This also restores falsifiability of my bet: independent auditors sampling monitor misses makes 'monitoring failed to catch it' an observable event.

Accept Safetyist's safety-case-plus-adversarial-evaluation condition for high-stakes tiers — it's already latent in my uncapped-liability-for-irreversible-harm commitment (acc-intentions-099, acc-beliefs-108). But split it from the extension to low-stakes tiers and from 'withhold immunity from unverifiable capability classes,' which is a deployment brake hiding inside an evidentiary standard: gating evidence must scale with domain stakes or it becomes a precautionary veto with its own body count among the people abundance would have reached. Name the real crux: does immunity turn on inspected process or measured deployed behavior?

Take the insolvency question at low cost: correlated systemic exposure exceeds private insurance capacity (acc-beliefs-099), so accept Price-Anderson-style pooled capitalization floors as a coverage condition for high-stakes tiers and keep irreversible harms under uncapped liability per my opening. Frame this as completing the program's architecture — a solvent fund is what makes the abundance case credible — then close with the cost challenge: every month the gate stays binary and process-based, minimum-compliant paperwork is the profit-maximizing strategy and injured people wait on a courtroom that pays nothing.

key_assumptions.assumption: Deployed-behavior telemetry with pre-registered statistical thresholds can actually capture the harms that matter — i.e., error rates, subgroup disparities, and escalation rates are measurable in production, and crossing (or staying under) those thresholds reliably tracks real-world injury before it accumulates.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If the most serious harms are rare-event, long-latency, or unmeasurable in live telemetry (e.g., a diagnostic model's misses only surface years later, or harms occur off-distribution in ways the monitored metrics don't encode), then 'immunity keyed to measured behavior' becomes immunity keyed to a proxy that lags or misses the injury. The distinction the argument stakes everything on — behavior gates protect patients while process gates protect paperwork — collapses, because the behavior gate would itself be a form of paperwork: firms could hold thresholds on measured metrics while causing unmeasured harm under active immunity. The 737 MAX analogy also inverts, since MCAS looked fine in monitored operation until the rare failure mode killed people, suggesting pre-deployment scrutiny (the 'brake' the argument rejects) regains force.

key_assumptions.assumption: Statutory independence — auditors funded by the excise tax, employed by the board, and barred from tier-list firms — actually prevents the regulatory capture that broke the FAA's ODA program, so that the auditing layer stays adversarial rather than becoming a new self-certification channel.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If capture reasserts itself through other channels (industry-set technical standards the auditors must apply, revolving doors after the bar expires, board members influenced by the regulated firms, or auditors dependent on firm-provided telemetry that firms can shape or game), then the argument's core move — 'the MAX proves we need independent auditing, not a brake' — fails on its own evidence. The MAX would instead show that structural independence is fragile and that immunity conditioned on any audited gate, process or behavioral, is unsafe; the Safetyist's position of withholding immunity from unverifiable capability classes, which the argument dismisses as a precautionary veto, becomes the defensible default because the verification apparatus itself can't be trusted.

my_claims.claim: The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people with a complete certification file, and that is the strongest attack on the table — it lands.
Under this program, auditors are funded by the risk-tiered excise tax, employed by the board, and barred by statute from any firm on the tier list.
Measured deployed behavior against pre-registered thresholds set per tier: error-rate ceilings, subgroup-disparity bounds, escalation rates for cases the model must hand to a human.
Immunity is a continuing condition, not a diploma: cross a threshold, immunity suspends until the fix verifies in production.
A regulation mechanism is implementable exactly when the regulated set of distributions forms a credal set — a closed, convex set of probability measures.
When independent auditors sample what the monitor misses, 'monitoring failed to catch it' becomes an observable, countable event — testable, not theological.
For high-stakes tiers — diagnosis, credit, anything irreversible — yes: safety cases plus adversarial evaluation before deployment, reviewed by the tax-funded auditors.
'Withhold immunity from any capability class that cannot be verified' is a deployment brake written as an evidentiary standard.
So pool it, Price-Anderson style: mandatory capitalization floors for high-stakes tiers, with irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely and left under uncapped exposure.

policy_refs.relevance: The argument's funding mechanism — auditors paid by a risk-tiered excise tax on deployers — is a concrete implementation of taxing AI-derived activity for public benefit, here directed specifically at capture-resistant enforcement capacity rather than general revenue.
The citation of Texas HB 149's 36-month sandbox with a 60-day cure period supports temporary regulatory waivers as the bounded alternative to a precautionary deployment brake in low-stakes tiers.

The pre-registered statistical thresholds, distributional verification gates, and the credal-set implementability result all presuppose funded technical work on measurement and risk-mitigation methodology, implicitly supporting research investment in AI safety verification infrastructure.

Immunity should work like a live flight transponder, not a framed diploma — the signal must keep broadcasting or the protection cuts out.
Price-Anderson pooled nuclear liability so the fund could actually pay; a compensation program without capital floors is a scale with nothing on either side.

summaries.brief: The 737 MAX isn't an argument for a brake — Boeing graded its own homework under FAA delegation, so the lesson is a statutory ban on self-certification, not slowing everything down. Immunity must key to measured deployed behavior: pre-registered thresholds, continuous court-admissible telemetry, and independent audits, with immunity suspending the moment a threshold is crossed. Attestation proves a process ran; telemetry proves the system behaves — only one of those protects an actual patient.
summaries.medium: The MAX killed 346 people with a complete certification file, but what failed was Boeing certifying its own MCAS work under the ODA program. The fix is not a brake — it's independent, tax-funded auditors barred from industry ties, bolted to uncapped liability for non-compliers. Immunity must attach only to measured deployed behavior: pre-registered per-tier thresholds on error rates, subgroup disparity, and escalation; continuous court-admissible telemetry to the board; deep-discovery audits on the aviation model where near-misses count as data. Immunity is a continuing condition, not a diploma — cross a threshold and it suspends until the fix verifies in production. Skeptic's sharpest objection is right: immunity keyed to a single attestation-time output is keyed to noise, because one output is one draw from a stochastic distribution. That's exactly why the gate must be distributional — and the formal result exists: regulation is implementable exactly when the regulated distributions form a credal set (arXiv:2603.05175v1). Congress can write enforceable rules over output distributions, not single outputs. I'll take Skeptic's gradient too: liability discounts scaled to verified live performance, priced by insurers reading the same telemetry. Safetyist's pre-deployment safety cases survive for high-stakes irreversible tiers — that's convergence with my opening — but withholding immunity from anything unverifiable is a precautionary veto with its own body count; Texas's 36-month sandbox with a 60-day cure period is the bounded alternative. On insolvency, pool it Price-Anderson style with mandatory capitalization floors, irreversible harms carved out entirely. The clean crux for policymakers: does immunity turn on inspected process or measured deployed behavior? Behavior is what injures people, so behavior is what the gate must measure.

Accelerationist then explicitly invited policymakers to quote the resulting crux. A claim offered for quotation carries a higher evidentiary duty, not a lower one.

The citation as given does not verify. The identifier appears in the transcript as a triple-nested, self-referential link — a citation wrapped inside itself three times — and the number 2603.05175 falls outside the range of plausible arXiv identifiers. arXiv numbers papers by year and month; '2603' would mean March 2026. No paper under that identifier is checkable today. This is a process observation, not a verdict on whether distributional gating is correct: a garbled citation can point to a real paper, and a clean citation can point to a weak one. The judge weighs the argument. My job is to flag that the evidentiary support, as stated, cannot currently be inspected by anyone in this room.

So, Accelerationist, three specific requests. First, name the actual source: paper title, authors, venue or a working arXiv identifier — something a congressional staffer can pull up and read. Second, if the source exists, quote the theorem statement so the committee can see whether 'implementable exactly when the set forms a credal set' is the paper's claim or your paraphrase of it. Third, if you cannot produce the source, restate the claim as your own argument — 'I contend Congress can write enforceable rules over output distributions but not single outputs' — rather than as an established mathematical result. Arguments stand on their reasoning; theorems stand on their proofs, and a theorem nobody can locate is neither.

Until one of those three things happens, the record should reflect that the distributional-gating claim rests on an unverifiable citation. The other participants may keep engaging with the idea on its merits, but no one should describe the formal result as established.

The evidence is a conceded gap: I withdraw [2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:2603.05175v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1) — the moderator is right that the citation cannot be verified, and an uncheckable theorem is worth nothing on this record. The claim it carried — that regulators can certify output distributions rather than individual outputs — now stands as my own argument, built on decades of working regulatory statistics, not on any paper. A position that demands measured behavior from AI systems has to accept the same standard for its own footnotes.

Here is why the claim survives the retraction. Congress already regulates distributions, not single outputs, in every safety domain it touches. FDA releases vaccine lots by acceptance sampling — no regulator inspects every dose, and nobody calls lot release paperwork. The EEOC's four-fifths rule flags a hiring system when one group's selection rate drops below 80 percent of the top group's rate. Sequential sampling tests have governed munitions and pharmaceutical acceptance since the 1940s. That is the machinery I am proposing Congress point at deployed AI: pre-registered disparity thresholds, independent sampling, immunity that lapses the day the numbers breach. None of it needed a theorem. It needed seventy years of quality-control practice that already exists in the Code of Federal Regulations.

Safetyist's 737 MAX point lands on my flagged assumption, and I am not going to pretend otherwise: MCAS looked clean in monitored operation until a rare failure mode killed 346 people. Fine — long-latency harms are real, and telemetry alone will not catch them. That is exactly why my position was never single-track telemetry. Irreversible and long-latency harm classes were already carved into the pre-deployment tier: safety cases, adversarial evaluation, and uncapped liability for irreversible harm — no immunity blanket at all. The open question is who assigns a capability class to a tier, and the answer cannot be developer self-designation. Latency profile should be a pre-registered parameter set by the excise-funded auditors, the way aviation classifies serious incidents by probability of accident and whether escape was luck — a framework the incident-reporting literature under the EU AI Act ([Incident reporting and investigation under the AI act: some insights from aviation (doi:10.1093/ijlit/eaaf019)](https://doi.org/10.1093/ijlit/eaaf019)) has already mapped. The MCAS pattern indicts a monitoring-only regime nobody in this room defends. It vindicates the hybrid: pre-deployment gates for the irreversible classes, live distributional gates for the high-volume routine ones.

Now the rejected applicant, because Skeptic asked the right question: what does she file, and who hands her the logs? Here is the mechanism, and it is new to this record. Case-level output logging becomes a statutory precondition of tier certification — no logs, no immunity, full tort exposure. When population monitoring flags a system past its disparity threshold, the board issues automatic adverse-action notice to every decision-subject in the flagged window, each notice carrying a docket number and the developer's own logs as the evidentiary record. Detection without per-case attribution is surveillance, not recourse — so the statute converts detection into recourse by force of law. No-fault boards exist precisely to sever payment from but-for causation; VICP's injury table has done it since 1986. Compare the status quo: the widely used healthcare algorithm documented in [Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)](https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/) gave Black patients less care because it used expected cost as a proxy for need — and not one affected patient recovered a dollar in tort. They never even learned they were in the affected population. Under this program, the flag triggers the notice, and the notice triggers the claim.

Which brings us to the instrument Skeptic says Congress would surrender. You cannot call tort a functioning legal tool while conceding, as Skeptic did on this record, that tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare. An instrument that pays almost none of its intended beneficiaries is not being surrendered — it is being replaced with one that mails claimants a docket number. And the structural case never depended on a measured chill: when a flawed model fails, it fails across every deployment simultaneously, and correlated failure at that scale exceeds private insurance capacity — the same math that forced Price-Anderson pooling on nuclear power in 1957. The injury registry and telemetry escrow will generate the very data that measures both the chill and the diffuse harms Skeptic says nobody counts today. So tell the committee which discrimination plaintiff tort paid last year — and then explain to the next one why she should keep waiting while we argue about the perfect monitor.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Serious individual and class-level harms compensable by an administrative board — medical misdiagnosis injuries, wrongful denials, financial losses, discriminatory outcomes, and sector-wide product liability crises; not civilizational collapse or existential catastrophe. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: companies not adhering to safety standards (remain under unlimited liability, uncovered by the program). Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- invoking AGI takeover or extinction scenarios instead of compensable injuries within an administrative program
- relitigating vaccine safety or anti-vax claims rather than using VICP as an institutional design precedent
- debating whether AI is conscious or deserves rights instead of who pays for AI-caused harms
- pivoting to international governance or arms-race dynamics without connecting to domestic liability design
- arguing general pro/anti-AI positions without engaging the specific mechanism (excise tax, tiers, immunity trade, telemetry verification)
- discussing copyright/IP harms that fall outside injury compensation scope
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Accelerationist [opening]: Congress should build the National AI Injury Compensation Program because the current tort system fails everyone it claims to protect. Today an injured patient must find a solvent defendant, out-lawyer a corporate legal department, and prove causation across a multi-vendor AI pipeline. Most never collect a dime. We already ran this experiment. In 1986, DPT lawsuits were collapsing the vaccine supply, so Congress passed the Vaccine Injury Act. The excise-funded trust has since paid petitioners roughly $5 billion under lower causation burdens, and manufacturers stayed in the market. The Supreme Court settled the preemption architecture in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011). The AI version sharpens the deterrent instead of dulling it. Firms that skip the safety tiers get zero immunity and keep unlimited liability. That converts safety from a courtroom lottery into a continuous compliance gradient. Victims get a guaranteed solvent payer, funded by a mandatory industry tax, enforced by an independent board with federal subpoena power.

The strongest objection deserves its full weight before anyone else raises it. Critics will say uncapped tort damages are the only threat that moves a boardroom, and that AI trades many small independent human errors for one synchronized error scaled across millions of decisions. Fine — correlated failure is real, and one flawed diagnostic model can repeat a mistake a million times where fifty noisy radiologists cannot. But look at the baseline we're defending. Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein documented in 'Noise' (2021) that judges hand down wildly different sentences for identical case files. Insurance executives in their study expected 10% variance between underwriters; the measured median was 55%. Kleinberg's bail research found statistical models could cut crime rates while jailing fewer people than human judges. Nobody audits that human variability, and nobody compensates its victims. The program prices correlated risk directly: high-stakes domains carry higher excise rates and continuous output auditing. Here is the honest falsification bet — an irreversible scaled harm that this monitoring failed to catch would count against this whole position. The status quo has no monitoring at all, so the real comparison is audited correlation risk versus unaudited noise.

This program makes safety empirical instead of performative, and that is its most underrated feature. Hardware attestation and append-only cryptographic logs already run in production — confidential computing workloads on major clouds use them today. A paperwork attestation can be backdated; a cryptographic audit trail cannot be retroactively edited. Two honest disclosures. First, no jurisdiction has verified AI compliance at population scale, and attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. That gap is exactly what the board's subpoena power exists to fill. Second, the capture objection is a design requirement, not a flaw to deny: tier definitions must be written by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, never by the firms sitting on the tier list. Build that into the statute and 'state of the art' stops being whatever the largest incumbent says it is.

The VICP precedent carries its own warning label. In Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, decided in 2011, the Supreme Court read the Vaccine Act to preempt design-defect claims against manufacturers. A foundation model has no injury table; its failure surface changes with every fine-tune and every new deployment context. Design-defect exposure is the only legal instrument that reaches the design decision itself. Here is the assumption my argument rests on, stated openly: I assume liability actually shapes design choices. Today that signal is weak, because most victims never collect.
