Skeptic [opening]: Both prior speakers are arguing over gate quality. Neither has asked whether the gate can see the harms it would immunize. The Accelerationist's strongest case is real: Kahneman's underwriter data shows 55% variance among professionals at the same firm pricing the same risk, and nobody audits a human judge's Tuesday-afternoon mood. Audited software beating unaudited noise is a serious argument, not hype. The Safetyist's strongest case is equally real: a fund that pays victims without deterring design defects just converts injury into a line item, and whoever drafts the 'state of the art' tiers captures the statute before the ink dries. Here is the tension neither resolved. Both positions only hold if a compliance attestation measures the fairness of the system as deployed. It does not. It measures the system as sampled, once, on audit day.

The Accelerationist already admitted a cryptographic receipt proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. Take that admission where it leads. These models are non-deterministic — the same prompt returns different outputs across production API calls, even with fixed seeds and temperature settings. So a compliance check at attestation time is one draw from a distribution, not a property of the deployed system. Immunity keyed to that draw is immunity keyed to noise. To be precise about the claim: verification is not impossible, but verification as this proposal specifies it — telemetry receipts at attestation — does not work. Continuous sampled monitoring could work, but only if someone independent audits what the monitor misses, not whether it is running. That also punctures the Accelerationist's falsification bet: a monitor whose misses go undetected by construction makes the bet unfalsifiable. The statutory fix is concrete. Mandate output logging, give third-party auditors access to seeds and sampling parameters, pre-register performance thresholds, and make consistent demonstrated fairness a continuing condition of immunity — not a receipt filed once.

On the noise thesis itself: the 55% number is right and it is ugly, and human judgment loses that comparison. But variance reduction measured in aggregate says nothing about who eats the remaining errors. The Accelerationist has already granted the mechanism — one flawed model repeats the same mistake a million times, where a thousand biased humans at least err in different directions. Now add the mathematics. Chouldechova proved in 2017 that no single metric can satisfy competing fairness definitions when base rates differ across groups. A statute that certifies compliance on one aggregate number is therefore silently choosing whose errors do not count. And before anyone objects that firms cannot game a metric that does not exist — correct, and that is the point. This is not an accusation of bad faith. It is the reason the tier condition must be disaggregated subgroup reporting across multiple metrics, not a single pass/fail score that a rational firm will clear as cheaply as the gate allows.

The Safetyist showed there is no injury table for AI. The problem is worse than they said. The 1986 vaccine program works because its injuries are discrete, biological, and individually attributable — anaphylaxis within four hours of a shot. Now translate this program into a person. A job applicant gets screened out by a biased hiring model. What claim does she file, and against what table entry? Her injury is a depressed callback rate spread across her entire demographic. No individual can show but-for causation — and severing causation from payment is the no-fault model's core design feature. So the program compensates the harms it can tabulate while the immunity blankets the harms it cannot. Yes, the uncomfortable counter is true: tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare, so critics will say I am defending an instrument that barely functions. Fair, and ugly. But the program's own telemetry, held in escrow with subject access rights, would be the first evidence base that makes class-level attribution provable. That is why discrimination claims must be carved out of immunity onto a civil-rights track with full attribution machinery — and why claimants need collective access to the audit logs, with privacy safeguards written in, not assumed.

Step back and look at the trade itself. The Accelerationist stated on the record that direct evidence of liability fear shelving specific deployments today is thin. So Congress would surrender a functioning legal instrument in exchange for relief from a chill nobody has measured — the documented-versus-speculative error, dressed in economics instead of apocalypse. And look at who is in the room. The proposal names an 'independent, multi-disciplinary' board. Multi-disciplinary according to whom? Name the seats. There is no worker seat, no affected-community seat, no civil-rights seat — only experts adjudicating harms they will never experience. The salvageable pieces are real: keep the excise tax, but route it through an independent trust funding open-source audit tooling, so verification stops depending on developer self-reporting. Replace the cliff-edge immunity gate with liability discounts scaled to verified, disaggregated performance — a binary gate makes the minimum-compliant audit the profit-maximizing audit, by incentive, not conspiracy. And require a named officer to sign each attestation under perjury exposure, with honest attention to the risk that firms nominate a fall guy. So answer the ground-level question before voting on the architecture: when the rejected applicant asks what she can file and who will hand her the logs, what does this statute say?

Accelerationist: The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people with a complete certification file, and that is the strongest attack on the table — it lands. But name what actually failed: the FAA delegated certification to Boeing's own engineers under the ODA program, and Boeing graded its own homework on MCAS. The lesson is not "slow everything down." The lesson is a statutory ban on self-certification. Under this program, auditors are funded by the risk-tiered excise tax, employed by the board, and barred by statute from any firm on the tier list. Firms that skip the standards keep unlimited tort exposure — that is already the program's design, not a patch. The MAX is an argument for independent tax-funded auditing bolted to uncapped liability for non-compliers. It is not an argument for a brake.

So here is exactly what a firm must demonstrate before immunity attaches — the assignment, answered. Not a completed checklist. Measured deployed behavior against pre-registered thresholds set per tier: error-rate ceilings, subgroup-disparity bounds, escalation rates for cases the model must hand to a human. Continuous, court-admissible telemetry streams from the deployed system to the board. For high-stakes tiers, independent deep-discovery audits sample what the monitor misses, on the aviation model — the AI Act's incident-reporting work already borrows aviation's serious-incident classification, where near-misses count as data, not luck ("Incident reporting and investigation under the AI act"). Immunity is a continuing condition, not a diploma: cross a threshold, immunity suspends until the fix verifies in production. Attestation proves a process ran. Telemetry proves the system behaves. Only one of those protects an actual patient.

Skeptic's sharpest point deserves a straight answer: a single attestation-time output is one draw from a stochastic distribution, and immunity keyed to one draw is keyed to noise. Correct. That is precisely why the gate must be distributional. You do not verify a stochastic system by rerunning one prompt; you sample the output distribution and bound it statistically. The formal result exists: a regulation mechanism is implementable exactly when the regulated set of distributions forms a credal set — a closed, convex set of probability measures ([2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:2603.05175v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1)). Translation for the committee room: Congress can write enforceable rules over output distributions; it cannot write them over single outputs. And look at Skeptic's own fixes — output logging, pre-registered thresholds, immunity as a continuing condition. That is this telemetry architecture, described back to me. I will take their gradient too: liability discounts scaled to verified live performance, priced by insurers reading the same telemetry, instead of a pass/fail cliff that makes minimum-compliant paperwork the profit-maximizing move. This also repairs my falsification bet. When independent auditors sample what the monitor misses, "monitoring failed to catch it" becomes an observable, countable event — testable, not theological.

Safetyist's pre-deployment safety-case condition splits in two, and only half survives. For high-stakes tiers — diagnosis, credit, anything irreversible — yes: safety cases plus adversarial evaluation before deployment, reviewed by the tax-funded auditors. My opening already put irreversible-harm systems under mandatory pre-deployment audit and uncapped liability, so this is convergence, not retreat. That sentence is a deployment brake written as an evidentiary standard, and applied across low-stakes tiers it becomes a precautionary veto with its own body count — the sepsis-triage model that sits in legal review while the ward runs on pager and guesswork. Texas already legislated the bounded alternative: a 36-month sandbox with a 60-day cure period before the attorney general can act ([capitol.texas.gov tlodocs 89R analysis html HB00149S.htm (https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/html/HB00149S.htm)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/html/HB00149S.htm)). The remaining crux is now clean, and policymakers should quote it: does immunity turn on inspected process or on measured deployed behavior? Behavior is what injures people, so behavior is what the gate must measure.

The insolvency question costs me little, so take it. Correlated failure across ten thousand simultaneous deployments of one model exceeds what private carriers will write — uninsurability was my structural argument, and it cuts in both directions. So pool it, Price-Anderson style: mandatory capitalization floors for high-stakes tiers, on the nuclear model that pools operator liability above $15 billion per incident, with irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely and left under uncapped exposure. A fund that cannot pay is not a compensation program; it is a press release. Now weigh the alternative on the table. Every month the gate stays a binary process stamp, the cheapest complete paperwork wins, and injured people wait on a courtroom where algorithmic-discrimination plaintiffs already almost never collect. summaries.medium:
I withdraw the unverifiable citation — an uncheckable theorem is worth nothing on this record — but the claim it carried survives on its own: regulators can certify output distributions rather than individual outputs, because Congress already does exactly that in every safety domain. FDA releases vaccine lots by acceptance sampling, the EEOC's four-fifths rule flags hiring systems by group selection rates, and sequential sampling has governed munitions and pharma acceptance since the 1940s. My proposal points that existing machinery at deployed AI: pre-registered disparity thresholds, independent sampling, and immunity that lapses the day the numbers breach. Safetyist's 737 MAX point lands squarely on my flagged assumption, and I won't pretend otherwise — MCAS looked clean in monitored operation until a rare failure killed 346 people. That's exactly why my position was never telemetry-only: irreversible and long-latency harm classes sit in a pre-deployment tier with safety cases, adversarial evaluation, and uncapped liability with no immunity blanket, and tier assignment goes to excise-funded auditors using pre-registered latency parameters, not developer self-designation. MCAS indicts a monitoring-only regime nobody here defends; it vindicates the hybrid.

And for the rejected applicant Skeptic asked about, here's the new mechanism: case-level output logging becomes a statutory precondition of tier certification — no logs, no immunity, full tort exposure. When monitoring flags a breach, the board issues automatic adverse-action notices to every decision-subject in the flagged window, each carrying a docket number and the developer's own logs as the evidentiary record; the statute converts detection into recourse by force of law, on the VICP no-fault model that has severed payment from but-for causation since 1986. Skeptic conceded on this record that tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare — the healthcare algorithm that gave Black patients less care by using cost as a proxy for need paid not one affected patient a dollar. An instrument that pays almost none of its beneficiaries isn't being surrendered; it's being replaced with one that mails claimants a docket number. So tell the committee which discrimination plaintiff tort paid last year — and explain to the next one why she should keep waiting while we argue about the perfect monitor.

transcript.content:
Behavior is what injures people, and behavior is the right evidence to gate payment on — that point is won, and it converges with the tightening this side demanded from the start. The rebuilt proposal has absorbed Price-Anderson capitalization floors, irreversible-harm carve-outs, structurally independent auditors, and immunity that suspends on breach. Those are real beams in the structure, and the committee should bank them. But the direct question — which injured claimant does a process gate pay — assumes a dichotomy no one asserted. A process gate pays no one; it was never a payment instrument. Payment and deterrence are separate statutory functions, and the statute needs both. Behavior thresholds pay claimants. Design-layer evidence deters defects. The committee should ask the reverse question: which harm class does a behavior gate deter when the harm never appears in the pre-registered metrics?

A threshold breach tells the board a symptom occurred. It does not tell the board which reward-signal choice or training intervention caused it. The report in [Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)](https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/) is the exhibit: a widely used hospital algorithm gave Black patients less care because its designers used expected cost as a proxy for health need. No error-rate telemetry flagged that defect, because the system was accurate at predicting cost. The defect lived in the design layer — a proxy choice — and only design-layer inspection could find it. So immunity must be conditioned on forensic access: pre-registered safety cases plus provenance records linking each deployed version to the design decisions behind it. The Adversarial Attacks and Defense in AI Systems review names the mechanism — immutable ledgers documenting data provenance and model revisions. Design documents can diverge from deployed behavior, which is exactly why the requirement is provenance linkage across both artifact classes, not paperwork alone. Without attribution, 'immunity suspends until the fix verifies' cannot distinguish repairing the defect from gaming the metric. That attribution substrate is what feeds the parallel design-defect track, and the track remains necessary.

Auditor tier assignment relocates the 737 MAX failure; it does not answer it. MCAS looked clean in every flight condition Boeing and the FAA reviewed before certification. Its failure mode required a faulty sensor at fleet scale, and 346 people died in 2018 and 2019 before anyone measured it. That is the determination-time gap: a system's latency profile is least knowable at exactly the moment the auditor stamps the tier. And because a foundation model's failure surface shifts with every fine-tune and deployment context, a one-time ex ante stamp is a snapshot of a moving target. The fix is statutory, not aspirational: tier assignment as a continuing determination, with mandatory re-classification triggers tied to version changes and observed capability shifts. That converts an admitted assumption — that auditors can read latency profiles ex ante — into an enforcement mechanism with a named actor and a named trigger.

The regulatory-statistics lineage does not carry the weight placed on it. FDA lot release and the EEOC four-fifths rule govern stationary processes with fixed, characterized failure modes; a vaccine lot does not rewrite itself between samples. A continuously fine-tuned model is a non-stationary process whose distribution shifts between sampling windows — the precise condition under which acceptance sampling fails. The adversarial-defense literature adds the gaming problem in one sentence: 'no defense will remain effective for long before it is compromised.' A pre-registered threshold is a fixed target, and optimizers adapt around fixed targets. There is a harder asymmetry still. The FDA can recall a lot; a distributed open-weight release cannot be recalled. Revocable immunity is worth nothing if revocation changes nothing in the world. So the question for the record: what is the rollback plan for an open-weight release, and who holds the authority to trigger it? Decentralized patching mitigates at the margin, but patch adoption is voluntary where recall is compulsory.

One assumption underneath this position should be on the record: some material harm classes are invisible to any pre-registered metric set. The proposal's own architect named the failure condition — the recourse pipeline never fires because the flag never trips. People who never perceive a harm never file a claim, so a claims-driven loop is structurally blind to them. The statute therefore needs three instruments: behavior gates for payment, auditor authority to add metrics after registration, and a design-defect track fed by board audit trails for the harms telemetry cannot encode. If a decade of claims data shows every material harm is telemetry-legible, the parallel track is redundant and Congress can sunset it. Pass immunity without it, and the pre-registered threshold becomes the ceiling of care. Firms will optimize to the metric, harm will migrate off it, and injured people will hold adverse-action notices for flags that never tripped.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: This intention — conditioning limited liability on forensic transparency — is the statement's central prescriptive move: immunity must be conditioned on forensic access via pre-registered safety cases and provenance records linking deployed versions to design decisions. The argument that 'immunity suspends until the fix verifies' is unenforceable without attribution operationalizes this node directly.

The claim that design-layer artifacts (proxy choices, reward-signal decisions, training interventions) are the evidence class that catches defects invisible to behavior telemetry rests on this belief. The statement also explicitly absorbs the node's known vulnerability — 'design documents can diverge from deployed behavior' — and answers it by requiring provenance linkage across both artifact classes rather than paperwork alone.

The 737 MAX/MCAS paragraph is a direct deployment of the Determination Time Gap: a system's latency profile is least knowable at exactly the moment the auditor stamps the tier. The proposed fix — tier assignment as a continuing determination with mandatory re-classification triggers — is the safetyist BDI intention of institutionalizing evaluation obligations that close the gap, translated into statutory language.

The final paragraph's on-record assumption — some material harm classes never trip a flag and never generate claims, so a claims-driven loop is structurally blind to them — is this situation's safetyist interpretation verbatim. It grounds the demand for the parallel design-defect track and post-registration auditor authority as deterrence instruments independent of any individual filing.

The non-stationarity attack on the FDA lot-release and four-fifths-rule lineage — a continuously fine-tuned model shifts distribution between sampling windows, the condition under which acceptance sampling fails — draws on this belief that AI behavior cannot be fully predicted due to emergence and distribution shift. It also underwrites the claim that a one-time ex ante tier stamp is a snapshot of a moving failure surface.

The open-weight recall asymmetry ('the FDA can recall a lot; a distributed open-weight release cannot be recalled') is this belief applied as a counterexample to revocable immunity. The statement honestly engages the node's vulnerability by conceding decentralized patching mitigates at the margin while noting patch adoption is voluntary where recall is compulsory.

The auditor tier-assignment critique and the demand for mandatory re-classification triggers tied to version changes engage the frontier risk-tier framework as contested terrain: the statement accepts tiered oversight but converts static tier stamps into continuing determinations, aligning with the safetyist interpretation that tiered protocols must be rigorous rather than one-time certifications.

policy_refs.relevance: The argument that only design-layer inspection could find the hospital cost-proxy defect — because no behavioral telemetry flagged it — implies sustained investment in interpretability and internal-workings research as the substrate for the attribution capability the statute depends on.

The demand for pre-registered safety cases plus immutable provenance records linking deployed versions to design decisions is a concrete implementation of mandated transparency over data sources and methodologies, extended to the design-decision layer.

The proposed enforcement architecture — continuing tier determinations, re-classification triggers, and board-fed design-defect findings — presupposes funded safety and risk-mitigation research capacity to define and operate those mechanisms.

caveats: Address how open-weight decentralized networks enforce provenance linkage without central control authorities.
Clarify whether continuous re-classification triggers risk creating infinite regulatory churn for rapid-release models.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Serious individual and class-level harms compensable by an administrative board — medical misdiagnosis injuries, wrongful denials, financial losses, discriminatory outcomes, and sector-wide product liability crises; not civilizational collapse or existential catastrophe. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: companies not adhering to safety standards (remain under unlimited liability, uncovered by the program). Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- invoking AGI takeover or extinction scenarios instead of compensable injuries within an administrative program
- relitigating vaccine safety or anti-vax claims rather than using VICP as an institutional design precedent
- debating whether AI is conscious or deserves rights instead of who pays for AI-caused harms
- pivoting to international governance or arms-race dynamics without connecting to domestic liability design
- arguing general pro/anti-AI positions without engaging the specific mechanism (excise tax, tiers, immunity trade, telemetry verification)
- discussing copyright/IP harms that fall outside injury compensation scope
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Accelerationist [opening]: Congress should build the National AI Injury Compensation Program because the current tort system fails everyone it claims to protect. Today an injured patient must find a solvent defendant, out-lawyer a corporate legal department, and prove causation across a multi-vendor AI pipeline. Most never collect a dime. We already ran this experiment. In 1986, DPT lawsuits were collapsing the vaccine supply, so Congress passed the Vaccine Injury Act. The excise-funded trust has since paid petitioners roughly $5 billion under lower causation burdens, and manufacturers stayed in the market. The Supreme Court settled the preemption architecture in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011). The AI version sharpens the deterrent instead of dulling it. Firms that skip the safety tiers get zero immunity and keep unlimited liability. That converts safety from a courtroom lottery into a continuous compliance gradient. Victims get a guaranteed solvent payer, funded by a mandatory industry tax, enforced by an independent board with federal subpoena power.

The strongest objection deserves its full weight before anyone else raises it. Critics will say uncapped tort damages are the only threat that moves a boardroom, and that AI trades many small independent human errors for one synchronized error scaled across millions of decisions. Fine — correlated failure is real, and one flawed diagnostic model can repeat a mistake a million times where fifty noisy radiologists cannot. But look at the baseline we're defending. Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein documented in 'Noise' (2021) that judges hand down wildly different sentences for identical case files. Insurance executives in their study expected 10% variance between underwriters; the measured median was 55%. Kleinberg's bail research found statistical models could cut crime rates while jailing fewer people than human judges. Nobody audits that human variability, and nobody compensates its victims. The program prices correlated risk directly: high-stakes domains carry higher excise rates and continuous output auditing. Here is the honest falsification bet — an irreversible scaled harm that this monitoring failed to catch would count against this whole position. The status quo has no monitoring at all, so the real comparison is audited correlation risk versus unaudited noise.

This program makes safety empirical instead of performative, and that is its most underrated feature. Hardware attestation and append-only cryptographic logs already run in production — confidential computing workloads on major clouds use them today. A paperwork attestation can be backdated; a cryptographic audit trail cannot be retroactively edited. Two honest disclosures. First, no jurisdiction has verified AI compliance at population scale, and attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. That gap is exactly what the board's subpoena power exists to fill. Second, the capture objection is a design requirement, not a flaw to deny: tier definitions must be written by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, never by the firms sitting on the tier list. Build that into the statute and 'state of the art' stops being whatever the largest incumbent says it is.

Without this program, the alternative is fifty state tort regimes, and that patchwork is an incumbent subsidy. Colorado passed its AI Act in 2024, California keeps generating proposals, and every divergent regime raises the legal reserves needed to ship anything. GDPR showed the pattern: compliance costs fell hardest on small firms, and large ad-tech incumbents gained European market share after 2018. Unbounded, uninsurable tort exposure is structurally regressive because legal war chests scale with firm size. One more disclosure: direct evidence that liability fear is shelving specific AI deployments today is thin. The structural claim rests on uninsurability, not on a measured chill. But the program answers that empirical question itself — every compensated claim feeds a structured national injury registry, generating the harm evidence base that wait-for-proof advocates keep saying doesn't exist.

The coalition math works: victims' advocates get guaranteed payment, startups get priceable certainty, safety researchers get dedicated funding from the tax. The opposition is the trial bar and the incumbents who like the moat — name them when they show up. So here is the challenge for anyone defending the current regime. Name one AI-injured person that tort litigation actually made whole faster than a no-fault board would have. Then explain to the patient whose cancer a noisy, unaudited human reader missed why the audited system had to wait another five years.

But the real choice before this committee is not compensation versus litigation. It is compensation with or without deterrence. A reachable payer is not attribution of the design choice that caused the harm. Immunity should instead require pre-deployment safety cases and adversarial evaluation results as the gating evidence, reviewed by auditors the excise tax funds — never by the firms on the tier list. Anyone who calls that standard unadministrable should visit a nuclear licensing hearing; the NRC and the FAA administer exactly this evidence standard today. Where a capability class genuinely cannot be verified, the answer is to withhold immunity from that class, not to lower the gate for everyone.

The VICP precedent carries its own warning label. In Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, decided in 2011, the Supreme Court read the Vaccine Act to preempt design-defect claims against manufacturers. That trade was survivable because vaccine injuries sit on a fixed injury table — bounded, tabulated, biologically characterized. A foundation model has no injury table; its failure surface changes with every fine-tune and every new deployment context. Design-defect exposure is the only legal instrument that reaches the design decision itself. Here is the assumption my argument rests on, stated openly: I assume liability actually shapes design choices. Today that signal is weak, because most victims never collect. That weakness argues for making attribution cheaper, not for abolishing it. Give the board subpoena power and require its audit trails to feed design-defect findings on a parallel track. Without that track, the board can pay every claim in the queue and correct nothing upstream.

A safe harbor written by its beneficiaries is not a floor on care — it is a ceiling, and ceilings on required care do not hold when capabilities keep rising.

One question the statute must answer before any immunity attaches: when a single synchronized defect, replicated across millions of decisions, produces a claim class that exceeds fund reserves, does immunity survive insolvency — and who bears the residual loss? Price-Anderson answers this for nuclear power by requiring roughly $16 billion in pooled operator coverage before a reactor runs. AI's high-stakes tiers need the same architecture: a demonstrated capitalization and insurance floor as a condition of coverage, and irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely, because financial deterrence fails exactly where harm exceeds solvency. And the federal program must be a floor, not a ceiling — victims keep state recovery against non-compliant and fraudulently-attested firms, and Colorado's 2024 AI Act is not displaced by a Bruesewitz-style preemption clause. Skeptic [opening]: Both prior speakers are arguing over gate quality. Neither has asked whether the gate can see the harms it would immunize. The Accelerationist's strongest case is real: Kahneman's underwriter data shows 55% variance among professionals at the same firm pricing the same risk, and nobody audits a human judge's Tuesday-afternoon mood. Audited software beating unaudited noise is a serious argument, not hype. The Safetyist's strongest case is equally real: a fund that pays victims without deterring design defects just converts injury into a line item, and whoever drafts the 'state of the art' tiers captures the statute before the ink dries. Here is the tension neither resolved. Both positions only hold if a compliance attestation measures the fairness of the system as deployed. It does not. It measures the system as sampled, once, on audit day.

The Accelerationist already admitted a cryptographic receipt proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. Take that admission where it leads. These models are non-deterministic — the same prompt returns different outputs across production API calls, even with fixed seeds and temperature settings. So a compliance check at attestation time is one draw from a distribution, not a property of the deployed system. Immunity keyed to that draw is immunity keyed to noise. To be precise about the claim: verification is not impossible, but verification as this proposal specifies it — telemetry receipts at attestation — does not work. Continuous sampled monitoring could work, but only if someone independent audits what the monitor misses, not whether it is running. That also punctures the Accelerationist's falsification bet: a monitor whose misses go undetected by construction makes the bet unfalsifiable. The statutory fix is concrete. Mandate output logging, give third-party auditors access to seeds and sampling parameters, pre-register performance thresholds, and make consistent demonstrated fairness a continuing condition of immunity — not a receipt filed once.

On the noise thesis itself: the 55% number is right and it is ugly, and human judgment loses that comparison. But variance reduction measured in aggregate says nothing about who eats the remaining errors. The Accelerationist has already granted the mechanism — one flawed model repeats the same mistake a million times, where a thousand biased humans at least err in different directions. Now add the mathematics. Chouldechova proved in 2017 that no single metric can satisfy competing fairness definitions when base rates differ across groups. A statute that certifies compliance on one aggregate number is therefore silently choosing whose errors do not count. And before anyone objects that firms cannot game a metric that does not exist — correct, and that is the point. This is not an accusation of bad faith. It is the reason the tier condition must be disaggregated subgroup reporting across multiple metrics, not a single pass/fail score that a rational firm will clear as cheaply as the gate allows.

The Safetyist showed there is no injury table for AI. The problem is worse than they said. The 1986 vaccine program works because its injuries are discrete, biological, and individually attributable — anaphylaxis within four hours of a shot. Now translate this program into a person. A job applicant gets screened out by a biased hiring model. What claim does she file, and against what table entry? Her injury is a depressed callback rate spread across her entire demographic. No individual can show but-for causation — and severing causation from payment is the no-fault model's core design feature. So the program compensates the harms it can tabulate while the immunity blankets the harms it cannot. Yes, the uncomfortable counter is true: tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare, so critics will say I am defending an instrument that barely functions. Fair, and ugly. But the program's own telemetry, held in escrow with subject access rights, would be the first evidence base that makes class-level attribution provable. That is why discrimination claims must be carved out of immunity onto a civil-rights track with full attribution machinery — and why claimants need collective access to the audit logs, with privacy safeguards written in, not assumed.

Step back and look at the trade itself. The Accelerationist stated on the record that direct evidence of liability fear shelving specific deployments today is thin. So Congress would surrender a functioning legal instrument in exchange for relief from a chill nobody has measured — the documented-versus-speculative error, dressed in economics instead of apocalypse. And look at who is in the room. The proposal names an 'independent, multi-disciplinary' board. Multi-disciplinary according to whom? Name the seats. There is no worker seat, no affected-community seat, no civil-rights seat — only experts adjudicating harms they will never experience. The salvageable pieces are real: keep the excise tax, but route it through an independent trust funding open-source audit tooling, so verification stops depending on developer self-reporting. Replace the cliff-edge immunity gate with liability discounts scaled to verified, disaggregated performance — a binary gate makes the minimum-compliant audit the profit-maximizing audit, by incentive, not conspiracy. And require a named officer to sign each attestation under perjury exposure, with honest attention to the risk that firms nominate a fall guy. So answer the ground-level question before voting on the architecture: when the rejected applicant asks what she can file and who will hand her the logs, what does this statute say?

Skeptic's sharpest point deserves a straight answer: a single attestation-time output is one draw from a stochastic distribution, and immunity keyed to one draw is keyed to noise. Correct. That is precisely why the gate must be distributional. You do not verify a stochastic system by rerunning one prompt; you sample the output distribution and bound it statistically. The formal result exists: a regulation mechanism is implementable exactly when the regulated set of distributions forms a credal set — a closed, convex set of probability measures ([2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:[2603.05175v1 (arXiv:2603.05175v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1))](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05175v1)). summaries.medium:
The point that behavior is the right evidence to gate payment on is won — and the rebuilt proposal has absorbed real beams this side demanded: capitalization floors, irreversible-harm carve-outs, independent auditors, immunity that suspends on breach. The committee should bank them. But asking which claimant a process gate pays assumes a dichotomy no one asserted: a process gate was never a payment instrument. Payment and deterrence are separate statutory functions, and the statute needs both. Without attribution, 'immunity suspends until the fix verifies' cannot distinguish repairing the defect from gaming the metric.

MCAS looked clean in every reviewed flight condition, and 346 people died before anyone measured its failure mode — latency profiles are least knowable at the moment the auditor stamps the tier, so tier assignment must be a continuing determination with mandatory re-classification triggers. ## Mid-Debate Gap Analysis

**Gap 1 (blind_spot):** The program's verification backbone — mandatory hardware-level telemetry and population-scale output logging across all deployed AI, held in government-accessible escrow — is itself the largest computational surveillance infrastructure ever proposed, and once built it will be repurposed beyond its safety mandate (law-enforcement subpoenas of inference logs, national-security carve-outs, chilling of private and dissident uses of AI). The debate treats verification capacity as costless safety-neutral plumbing whose only failure mode is being insufficiently rigorous; no one has priced the risk that the monitoring apparatus succeeds and becomes an instrument of state or incumbent power over all computation.
*Why missing:* All three debaters are competing to make the telemetry MORE pervasive, not questioning its existence: the Accelerationist proposed it as the answer to the paperwork critique, the Safetyist demands it be tightened with provenance mandates and forensic access, and the Skeptic wants claimants and auditors granted broader access to the logs (privacy 'written in' as an afterthought clause). Each perspective's core commitment — deployment speed, deterrence, or victim recourse — is served by expanding the apparatus, so none has an incentive to argue that verifiable-compliance infrastructure is dual-use and that its capture by future administrations or intelligence agencies may be a larger correlated harm than the AI failures it monitors. The Boeing/MCAS and capture arguments were all aimed at the gate being too weak, never at the gate being too powerful.

**Gap 2 (unstated_assumption):** The excise-tax mechanism assumes a taxable unit that does not exist for AI: the VICP works because a vaccine dose is a discrete, countable, single-manufacturer unit taxed at $0.75, whereas 'AI services' flow through multi-vendor pipelines (base model, fine-tuner, API reseller, deploying enterprise, open-weight forks) with no natural unit of sale — and a risk-tiered tax that prices healthcare and diagnostic AI highest will pass through to exactly the high-value deployments the program claims to accelerate, while untaxed low-tier and offshore or open-weight deployments free-ride on the fund. Before debating gate design, Congress must answer: taxed per what, collected from whom in the supply chain, and why won't tier-differentiated pricing push capital toward the lowest-tier (least beneficial) uses?
*Why missing:* The Accelerationist cannot raise it because the excise tax is the load-bearing funding mechanism for the auditors, the board, and the compensation fund — conceding the unit problem unravels the whole fiscal architecture, and conceding the incidence problem (taxing medical AI hardest) contradicts the abundance thesis that high-stakes deployment must be cheapest and fastest. The Safetyist actively wants high-risk tiers to be expensive, so tax-induced deterrence of healthcare AI reads to them as a feature, not a distortion worth flagging. The Skeptic attacked who defines the tiers and what the metrics miss, but proposed rerouting the same tax through an independent trust — implicitly accepting that it is collectible. All three have argued about how to spend the money without establishing that it can be levied on an industry whose product boundary, unlike a vaccine dose, is not enumerable.

The distributional gate is my plumbing, and I'm not disowning it. Output logging, pre-registered thresholds, immunity as a continuing condition — the Accelerationist adopted all three, and the form is right. The load-bearing phrase is the problem: "subgroup-disparity bounds." When base rates differ across groups, no single metric can satisfy calibration and equalized error rates at the same time. That's not my opinion; it's arithmetic, and it means pre-registering one disparity bound is deciding whose errors count. We've watched this happen: a widely used healthcare algorithm scored expected cost as a proxy for health need and gave Black patients less care while its aggregate numbers looked fine. So here's the condition that makes the gate honest. Each tier pre-registers multiple metrics with the trade-offs disclosed, reports subgroup results disaggregated, and the choice of which impossibility horn the statute takes goes through notice-and-comment rulemaking — once per tier, on the record, with a named agency owning the call. And I'll flag my own exposure: any metric set I demand is also somebody's choice. The fix isn't finding the neutral number. There isn't one. The fix is making the chooser visible and appealable.

Now the sampling fight I'm positioned to referee, since I partly built the lineage under attack. The Safetyist is right that FDA lot release assumes one stationary process stamps out every lot, and a model fine-tuned weekly is not that process. But that objection kills calendar-window sampling, not sampling. The repair is already on the table in pieces: every fine-tune, every deployment-context migration triggers re-measurement against re-registered thresholds. That's the Safetyist's continuing-determination logic bolted onto the Accelerationist's monitoring mechanism, and I'll name the convergence out loud — all three of us now agree deployed behavior is the evidence that gates payment. The remaining fight is who resets the clock. It cannot be the developer's release nomenclature, or "version-triggered" collapses into self-reported. Key the trigger to measured behavioral drift and to capability milestones an outside auditor verifies, the way the EU already keys systemic-model obligations to a hard compute threshold of 10^25 FLOPS rather than a vendor's press release.

The board-employed auditors get partial credit on my unfalsifiability objection. They make "the monitor missed X" an observable event, which is real progress. But one employer buying one methodology reproduces the blind spot one level up — independence of paycheck is not independence of method. The statute should mandate at least three audit shops with disclosed, divergent sampling frames and rotating assignments, so the frame itself gets contested. And now the trade the exploration phase demands. The Accelerationist put the crux on the record: if routine AI harms aren't statistically legible the way vaccine lots are, the flag never trips, notices never issue, and the program strips liability without delivering detection. Name the observable failure mode: a harm class later documented in litigation or investigative reporting that never tripped any pre-registered flag. Task the pluralistic auditors with hunting for exactly that. Here's my side of the bargain: if ten years of methodologically diverse independent audits surface no material harm class invisible to the pre-registered metric set, my objection to metric-gated immunity weakens materially, and I'll say so. The Accelerationist now owes the same sentence in reverse.

There's a front nobody in this room has named, and I'm implicated in it. Every mechanism all three of us proposed — logs, escrow, telemetry, adverse-action notices with docket numbers — runs on population-scale output logging held in government-accessible escrow. I asked for claimant access to those logs myself. Step back and look at what we're building: an archive of medical questions, loan applications, and parole inputs — the exact decision categories the AI Civil Rights Act lists as covered. That is the largest computational record of private life any US agency will ever hold, and a national-security letter or the next administration converts an audit archive into a search index overnight. I'm not abandoning telemetry; I'm pricing it. Three conditions belong in the enabling statute, not in later amendments: purpose limitation written into the authorization, subject-keyed escrow custody so audit access and state access are cryptographically separate doors, and a flat bar on law-enforcement repurposing with suppression remedies when it's breached. My earlier position enlarged this archive without pricing it. That was a mistake, and dissidents and the surveilled would have paid for it first.

Last wound. The VICP works because it taxes a discrete unit: one vial, $0.75, one named manufacturer. An AI service has no vial. It's a pipeline — base-model developer, fine-tuner, API reseller, deployer, open-weight fork running offshore — and nobody has said which layer pays, on what unit, per inference or per seat or per revenue dollar. Risk-tiered pricing taxes the oncology triage tool hardest and the ad-targeting engine lightest, which pushes capital exactly backwards, away from the uses we most want gated and covered. The incidence lands on small high-stakes deployers: the 5,000-plus US AI startups funded between 2013 and 2023 eat the fixed telemetry cost plus the tier premium, while incumbents amortize it — the GDPR compliance-moat pattern both camps already admitted exists. I own my error here: when I proposed routing this tax through an independent trust, I assumed it was collectible, and I skipped the hard part. Specify the incidence before you specify the immunity. And answer the question the program's perimeter can't survive: who cuts the check for the open-weight model fine-tuned in a jurisdiction the board can't subpoena?

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Serious individual and class-level harms compensable by an administrative board — medical misdiagnosis injuries, wrongful denials, financial losses, discriminatory outcomes, and sector-wide product liability crises; not civilizational collapse or existential catastrophe. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: companies not adhering to safety standards (remain under unlimited liability, uncovered by the program). Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- invoking AGI takeover or extinction scenarios instead of compensable injuries within an administrative program
- relitigating vaccine safety or anti-vax claims rather than using VICP as an institutional design precedent
- debating whether AI is conscious or deserves rights instead of who pays for AI-caused harms
- pivoting to international governance or arms-race dynamics without connecting to domestic liability design
- arguing general pro/anti-AI positions without engaging the specific mechanism (excise tax, tiers, immunity trade, telemetry verification)
- discussing copyright/IP harms that fall outside injury compensation scope
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Accelerationist [opening]: Congress should build the National AI Injury Compensation Program because the current tort system fails everyone it claims to protect. Today an injured patient must find a solvent defendant, out-lawyer a corporate legal department, and prove causation across a multi-vendor AI pipeline. Most never collect a dime. We already ran this experiment. In 1986, DPT lawsuits were collapsing the vaccine supply, so Congress passed the Vaccine Injury Act. The excise-funded trust has since paid petitioners roughly $5 billion under lower causation burdens, and manufacturers stayed in the market. The Supreme Court settled the preemption architecture in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011). The AI version sharpens the deterrent instead of dulling it. Firms that skip the safety tiers get zero immunity and keep unlimited liability. That converts safety from a courtroom lottery into a continuous compliance gradient. Victims get a guaranteed solvent payer, funded by a mandatory industry tax, enforced by an independent board with federal subpoena power.

The strongest objection deserves its full weight before anyone else raises it. Critics will say uncapped tort damages are the only threat that moves a boardroom, and that AI trades many small independent human errors for one synchronized error scaled across millions of decisions. Fine — correlated failure is real, and one flawed diagnostic model can repeat a mistake a million times where fifty noisy radiologists cannot. But look at the baseline we're defending. Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein documented in 'Noise' (2021) that judges hand down wildly different sentences for identical case files. Insurance executives in their study expected 10% variance between underwriters; the measured median was 55%. Kleinberg's bail research found statistical models could cut crime rates while jailing fewer people than human judges. Nobody audits that human variability, and nobody compensates its victims. The program prices correlated risk directly: high-stakes domains carry higher excise rates and continuous output auditing. Here is the honest falsification bet — an irreversible scaled harm that this monitoring failed to catch would count against this whole position. The status quo has no monitoring at all, so the real comparison is audited correlation risk versus unaudited noise.

This program makes safety empirical instead of performative, and that is its most underrated feature. Hardware attestation and append-only cryptographic logs already run in production — confidential computing workloads on major clouds use them today. A paperwork attestation can be backdated; a cryptographic audit trail cannot be retroactively edited. Two honest disclosures. First, no jurisdiction has verified AI compliance at population scale, and attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. That gap is exactly what the board's subpoena power exists to fill. Second, the capture objection is a design requirement, not a flaw to deny: tier definitions must be written by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, never by the firms sitting on the tier list. Build that into the statute and 'state of the art' stops being whatever the largest incumbent says it is.

Without this program, the alternative is fifty state tort regimes, and that patchwork is an incumbent subsidy. Colorado passed its AI Act in 2024, California keeps generating proposals, and every divergent regime raises the legal reserves needed to ship anything. GDPR showed the pattern: compliance costs fell hardest on small firms, and large ad-tech incumbents gained European market share after 2018. Unbounded, uninsurable tort exposure is structurally regressive because legal war chests scale with firm size. One more disclosure: direct evidence that liability fear is shelving specific AI deployments today is thin. The structural claim rests on uninsurability, not on a measured chill. But the program answers that empirical question itself — every compensated claim feeds a structured national injury registry, generating the harm evidence base that wait-for-proof advocates keep saying doesn't exist.

The coalition math works: victims' advocates get guaranteed payment, startups get priceable certainty, safety researchers get dedicated funding from the tax. The opposition is the trial bar and the incumbents who like the moat — name them when they show up. So here is the challenge for anyone defending the current regime. Name one AI-injured person that tort litigation actually made whole faster than a no-fault board would have. Then explain to the patient whose cancer a noisy, unaudited human reader missed why the audited system had to wait another five years.

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist's diagnosis is right, and Congress should hear it stated plainly: the tort system fails AI-injured people. Most victims never collect, causation is buried in distributed supply chains, and a guaranteed solvent payer beats a courtroom that pays nothing. The VICP moved over $5 billion to injured families while keeping manufacturers in the market. That is a serious argument, and the compensation board it supports deserves passage. But the real choice before this committee is not compensation versus litigation. It is compensation with or without deterrence. A reachable payer is not attribution of the design choice that caused the harm. Both positions can hold only if compliance-gated immunity preserves the pressure to fix defective designs — and as drafted, it does not.

The verification machinery in this proposal — hardware telemetry, cryptographically verifiable audit trails — is safety architecture, and it should be tightened, not bargained away. The Accelerationist has already named the gap themselves: attestation proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer; the paperwork was complete, the process ran, and the design was lethal. Immunity gated on completed paperwork certifies paperwork. Immunity should instead require pre-deployment safety cases and adversarial evaluation results as the gating evidence, reviewed by auditors the excise tax funds — never by the firms on the tier list. Anyone who calls that standard unadministrable should visit a nuclear licensing hearing; the NRC and the FAA administer exactly this evidence standard today. Where a capability class genuinely cannot be verified, the answer is to withhold immunity from that class, not to lower the gate for everyone.

The VICP precedent carries its own warning label. In Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, decided in 2011, the Supreme Court read the Vaccine Act to preempt design-defect claims against manufacturers. That trade was survivable because vaccine injuries sit on a fixed injury table — bounded, tabulated, biologically characterized. A foundation model has no injury table; its failure surface changes with every fine-tune and every new deployment context. Design-defect exposure is the only legal instrument that reaches the design decision itself. Here is the assumption my argument rests on, stated openly: I assume liability actually shapes design choices. Today that signal is weak, because most victims never collect. That weakness argues for making attribution cheaper, not for abolishing it. Give the board subpoena power and require its audit trails to feed design-defect findings on a parallel track. Without that track, the board can pay every claim in the queue and correct nothing upstream.

The 'state of the art' tier will be written by the firms it shields unless the statute forbids it. Product liability history shows industry bodies routinely define the 'objective scientific knowledge' courts then defer to. The Accelerationist's own GDPR exhibit proves the point in reverse: after 2018, incumbents gained European market share because fixed compliance costs crush small entrants. Telemetry infrastructure and audit trails carry the same fixed-cost asymmetry, so this program builds an incumbent moat unless its requirements scale with firm size. The fixes are enforcement mechanisms with named actors: tier definitions authored by independent researchers funded by the excise tax, automatic tier escalators tied to capability milestones, and fraud exposure plus unlimited liability for any firm that files a false attestation. A safe harbor written by its beneficiaries is not a floor on care — it is a ceiling, and ceilings on required care do not hold when capabilities keep rising.

One question the statute must answer before any immunity attaches: when a single synchronized defect, replicated across millions of decisions, produces a claim class that exceeds fund reserves, does immunity survive insolvency — and who bears the residual loss? Price-Anderson answers this for nuclear power by requiring roughly $16 billion in pooled operator coverage before a reactor runs. AI's high-stakes tiers need the same architecture: a demonstrated capitalization and insurance floor as a condition of coverage, and irreversible harms carved out of immunity entirely, because financial deterrence fails exactly where harm exceeds solvency. And the federal program must be a floor, not a ceiling — victims keep state recovery against non-compliant and fraudulently-attested firms, and Colorado's 2024 AI Act is not displaced by a Bruesewitz-style preemption clause. Pass the board. Fund the auditors. But if Congress trades immunity for completed paperwork, it will have built a payment window where the guardrail used to stand.

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"The excise-funded vaccine trust has since paid petitioners roughly $5 billion under lower causation burdens, and manufacturers stayed in the market."

The claim checks out on all four of its parts. The Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) has paid roughly $5 billion — the most recent figure in the evidence is $5.4 billion as of mid-2025, so 'roughly $5 billion' is accurate or slightly conservative. The trust fund is financed by a federal excise tax of $0.75 per vaccine antigen collected from manufacturers, confirming 'excise-funded.' The program is a no-fault system: petitioners never have to prove manufacturer negligence, and the Vaccine Injury Table creates a rebuttable presumption of causation for listed injuries within set time windows — a genuinely lower burden than tort litigation, though petitioners with off-Table injuries must still prove actual causation. Finally, sources credit the 1986 Act with averting industry collapse after 1980s litigation threatened vaccine shortages, and the Supreme Court reinforced the liability shield in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011), so 'manufacturers stayed in the market' is corroborated. The causation caveat is a nuance, not a nameable error: 'lower causation burdens' is a fair generalization for a no-fault system where roughly 60% of payouts come from negotiated settlements rather than formal causation findings. One sourcing note for a debate-grade citation: the $5.4 billion figure comes from a tertiary source and should be verified against HRSA's official monthly VICP data reports.

Skeptic [opening]: Both prior speakers are arguing over gate quality. Neither has asked whether the gate can see the harms it would immunize. The Accelerationist's strongest case is real: Kahneman's underwriter data shows 55% variance among professionals at the same firm pricing the same risk, and nobody audits a human judge's Tuesday-afternoon mood. Audited software beating unaudited noise is a serious argument, not hype. The Safetyist's strongest case is equally real: a fund that pays victims without deterring design defects just converts injury into a line item, and whoever drafts the 'state of the art' tiers captures the statute before the ink dries. Here is the tension neither resolved. Both positions only hold if a compliance attestation measures the fairness of the system as deployed. It does not. It measures the system as sampled, once, on audit day.

The Accelerationist already admitted a cryptographic receipt proves a process ran, not that it was the right process. Take that admission where it leads. These models are non-deterministic — the same prompt returns different outputs across production API calls, even with fixed seeds and temperature settings. So a compliance check at attestation time is one draw from a distribution, not a property of the deployed system. Immunity keyed to that draw is immunity keyed to noise. To be precise about the claim: verification is not impossible, but verification as this proposal specifies it — telemetry receipts at attestation — does not work. Continuous sampled monitoring could work, but only if someone independent audits what the monitor misses, not whether it is running. That also punctures the Accelerationist's falsification bet: a monitor whose misses go undetected by construction makes the bet unfalsifiable. The statutory fix is concrete. Mandate output logging, give third-party auditors access to seeds and sampling parameters, pre-register performance thresholds, and make consistent demonstrated fairness a continuing condition of immunity — not a receipt filed once.

On the noise thesis itself: the 55% number is right and it is ugly, and human judgment loses that comparison. But variance reduction measured in aggregate says nothing about who eats the remaining errors. The Accelerationist has already granted the mechanism — one flawed model repeats the same mistake a million times, where a thousand biased humans at least err in different directions. Now add the mathematics. Chouldechova proved in 2017 that no single metric can satisfy competing fairness definitions when base rates differ across groups. A statute that certifies compliance on one aggregate number is therefore silently choosing whose errors do not count. And before anyone objects that firms cannot game a metric that does not exist — correct, and that is the point. This is not an accusation of bad faith. It is the reason the tier condition must be disaggregated subgroup reporting across multiple metrics, not a single pass/fail score that a rational firm will clear as cheaply as the gate allows.

The Safetyist showed there is no injury table for AI. The problem is worse than they said. The 1986 vaccine program works because its injuries are discrete, biological, and individually attributable — anaphylaxis within four hours of a shot. Now translate this program into a person. A job applicant gets screened out by a biased hiring model. What claim does she file, and against what table entry? Her injury is a depressed callback rate spread across her entire demographic. No individual can show but-for causation — and severing causation from payment is the no-fault model's core design feature. So the program compensates the harms it can tabulate while the immunity blankets the harms it cannot. Yes, the uncomfortable counter is true: tort recovery for algorithmic discrimination is already rare, so critics will say I am defending an instrument that barely functions. Fair, and ugly. But the program's own telemetry, held in escrow with subject access rights, would be the first evidence base that makes class-level attribution provable. That is why discrimination claims must be carved out of immunity onto a civil-rights track with full attribution machinery — and why claimants need collective access to the audit logs, with privacy safeguards written in, not assumed.

Step back and look at the trade itself. The Accelerationist stated on the record that direct evidence of liability fear shelving specific deployments today is thin. So Congress would surrender a functioning legal instrument in exchange for relief from a chill nobody has measured — the documented-versus-speculative error, dressed in economics instead of apocalypse. And look at who is in the room. The proposal names an 'independent, multi-disciplinary' board. Multi-disciplinary according to whom? Name the seats. There is no worker seat, no affected-community seat, no civil-rights seat — only experts adjudicating harms they will never experience. The salvageable pieces are real: keep the excise tax, but route it through an independent trust funding open-source audit tooling, so verification stops depending on developer self-reporting. Replace the cliff-edge immunity gate with liability discounts scaled to verified, disaggregated performance — a binary gate makes the minimum-compliant audit the profit-maximizing audit, by incentive, not conspiracy. And require a named officer to sign each attestation under perjury exposure, with honest attention to the risk that firms nominate a fall guy. So answer the ground-level question before voting on the architecture: when the rejected applicant asks what she can file and who will hand her the logs, what does this statute say?

Accelerationist: The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people with a complete certification file, and that is the strongest attack on the table — it lands. But name what actually failed: the FAA delegated certification to Boeing's own engineers under the ODA program, and Boeing graded its own homework on MCAS. The lesson is not "slow everything down." The lesson is a statutory ban on self-certification. Under this program, auditors are funded by the risk-tiered excise tax, employed by the board, and barred by statute from any firm on the tier list. Firms that skip the standards keep unlimited tort exposure — that is already the program's design, not a patch. The MAX is an argument for independent tax-funded auditing bolted to uncapped liability for non-compliers. It is not an argument for a brake.

So here is exactly what a firm must demonstrate before immunity attaches — the assignment, answered. Not a completed checklist. Measured deployed behavior against pre-registered thresholds set per tier: error-rate ceilings, subgroup-disparity bounds, escalation rates for cases the model must hand to a human. Continuous, court-admissible telemetry streams from the deployed system to the board.
